content: Any operational or procedural characteristics of diagnostic products that do not align with the manufacturer’s claims should be documented and reported in accordance with the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on post-market surveillance for in vitro diagnostics. A false-negative HIV result typically occurs when one diagnostic product (commonly referred to as Assay 1) fails to detect HIV. However, such errors are often difficult to identify unless an individual with a known HIV-positive status undergoes retesting. It is important to note that WHO does not recommend retesting for individuals already diagnosed as HIV-positive, especially those on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Conversely, a false-positive HIV result may arise from one or more products in the testing algorithm, often involving Assay 2 or Assay 3. To address this, WHO recommends retesting individuals before initiating ART to identify those who may have been incorrectly diagnosed as HIV-positive. The accuracy of testing algorithms should be routinely evaluated through post-market surveillance. Complaints related to diagnostic products should be reported to both the assay manufacturer and the national regulatory authority as part of post-market surveillance efforts. Quality management systems are essential for all aspects of HIV testing services (HTS), whether conducted in laboratories, health facilities, or community-based settings. This includes rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) performed by lay providers. In vitro diagnostics (IVDs) used for HIV testing must meet regulatory standards as outlined in national guidelines. WHO conducts independent prequalification assessments of IVDs, with a focus on RDTs and other diagnostics intended for use in resource-limited settings. In some cases, HTS providers may refer individuals to another site for additional testing to confirm their HIV status. Accurate, confidential, and timely record-keeping is critical at both the initial testing site and the referral site. Ensuring timely, affordable, and accurate HIV diagnosis is a cornerstone of any HIV program. It is vital to organize and manage HTS so that all individuals with HIV are diagnosed and successfully linked to treatment and care, regardless of their economic or social status or geographic location. This is particularly important in the context of the “treat all” recommendations for initiating ART. Care must be taken to avoid misdiagnosing individuals without HIV as HIV-positive, which could lead to unnecessary lifelong ART. Similarly, individuals with HIV must not be misdiagnosed as HIV-negative, as this would prevent them from accessing treatment and increase the risk of onward transmission. Recent global reports indicate that the quality of HTS is suboptimal in some settings, with issues such as the use of non-recommended testing strategies, user errors, and inadequate supervision of testing facilities contributing to poor outcomes. To address these challenges, HTS programs must implement robust quality management systems, regardless of the testing location or personnel involved. This includes ensuring that testing sites are well-stocked, staff are adequately trained, and testing services are accessible and reliable. Quality management encompasses quality assurance, quality control, and quality improvement, focusing on the processes required for effective testing rather than just the quality of the diagnostic products used. National policies, strategic plans, and monitoring processes are critical for supporting quality management systems at testing sites. Testing strategies and algorithms should align with WHO recommendations, and pre-market assessments should identify high-quality IVDs. Post-market surveillance, including reporting complaints and participating in external quality assessment (EQA) schemes, is necessary to maintain high standards. Additionally, uninterrupted supply chains and proper storage of test kits are crucial for effective HTS. In summary, ensuring the quality of HIV testing services requires a comprehensive approach that includes adherence to international standards, effective training and supervision of staff, robust quality management systems, and continuous monitoring and improvement of testing processes.
